sections.h2: Which Rye does this page cover?
sections.html:
This page covers the Town of Rye in Westchester County, which is a different municipality from the City of Rye. The town is made up of the Village of Port Chester, the Village of Rye Brook and the Rye Neck section of the Village of Mamaroneck, and it holds around 11,000 parcels. The City of Rye became independent in 1942, so a house inside the city is handled by city offices, and the town assessor has no file on it.

The town comes in two separate pieces: Rye Neck lies to the southwest, apart from Rye Brook and Port Chester. Work out which village your street belongs to first. That one fact tells you who issues permits, who bills the village portion of your tax and which building department holds your certificate of occupancy.

The mid-2025 population is 50,011, up 0.8% from 2020. The town sits about 30 miles north of New York City on Long Island Sound, with two Metro-North stations and I-95 nearby.

sections.h2: What are the ways to sell fast?
sections.html:
Speed here comes down to two things: the shape the house is in and the date you need the money.

  • Broker listing: suits a house that photographs well, if you can live with showings and a buyer's mortgage clock. A written net-proceeds estimate shows what you keep.
  • Owner-handled sale: no broker fee, but you field every inquiry and negotiate the contract with your own attorney.
  • Investor purchase for cash: the buyer takes the property as is. Estates, tenant-occupied two-families, and houses carrying open violations are the usual candidates.

At Westchester prices, a few percentage points between a listing and a cash offer become real money, so line up the final check from each path.

Owners live in 57.9% of the town's homes, and the middle owner-occupied value is $689,400. Median monthly owner costs with a mortgage are reported as $4,000 or more, the top reporting band.

With 49.7% of residents aged 5 and over speaking a language other than English at home, a listing that offers a bilingual contact can reach more of the buyers who live nearby.

The town values property at 100% of market value, so the number on your assessment should match what the house would bring. The cycle runs on a handful of dates.

  • May 1 is taxable status date, and also the cutoff for exemption filings.
  • The tentative roll is posted June 1, and grievance day falls on the third Tuesday of June.
  • Decisions from the Board of Assessment Review are mailed around September 15, when the final roll is filed.
  • Billing years differ by levy: county and town taxes follow the calendar year, village taxes run June to May, and school taxes run July to June.

The Receiver of Taxes takes payments and mail at 222 Grace Church Street, third floor, Port Chester. The Port Chester and Rye Brook village bills are each paid in two installments with their own windows.

Submit Form RP-524 to the assessment office by hand, through the secure drop box, or as a PDF by email to the address on the town's page. A mailed form has to be in the office by 8 p.m. on grievance day, and a postmark that same day is late. Owners of one-to-three-family homes who disagree with the board can file a small claims petition electronically with the county clerk within 30 days of the final roll, which puts the deadline on October 15.

The assessor needs exemption applications and renewals, senior citizen ones included, by May 1 each year. Basic and Enhanced STAR have moved to the state: new homeowners register with the Department of Taxation and Finance, and the town's assessor no longer takes STAR forms.

Limited-income seniors, owners with Cold War or alternative military-service exemptions, and volunteer firefighters can apply through the assessor. Tell your buyer early so they do not assume your current bill carries over untouched.

sections.h2: Permits and the certificate of occupancy
sections.html:
The town has no building or planning department of its own. Each village runs those functions, so your village building department holds the permits and the certificate of occupancy.

The assessor's property record card shows the use the assessor knows about, but it is not proof of legal use. Before listing, look for these:

  • Permits and final sign-offs for any addition, finished basement or garage conversion.
  • The certificate of occupancy, which states the authorized use.
  • Zoning district and map, which come from the village building or planning office.
  • Radius and abutter search instructions, which also come from the village building department.

A cash buyer can often take the house with a paperwork gap still open, though the offer will reflect the cost of curing it.

Westchester's County Clerk records the deed through its online PREP portal, which also builds the cover page, the state TP-584 and the RP-5217 report. For a residential deed in a single municipality the fees are a $45 statutory fee, $5 a page, $5 for the TP-584 and $125 for the RP-5217.

State transfer tax adds $2 for each $500 of price, rounded up. The 1% mansion tax starts at $1 million and falls on the buyer. The clerk accepts transfer tax by ACH, certified or bank check, attorney escrow check or a check from an approved vendor, while credit cards cover fees only.

Once you accept an offer, the work splits between you, your attorney and the village. You gather the permit file and certificate of occupancy from your village building department. Your attorney asks the Receiver of Taxes for the current balances on the county, town, village and school bills. The buyer's side orders title work and, for a mortgage buyer, an appraisal. A cash buyer skips those last two, so title and the village paperwork set the pace.

At closing you sign the deed. It then goes through the county's PREP portal, where the cover page, the TP-584 and the RP-5217 are built together. Because Port Chester, Rye Brook and Rye Neck each bill separately, ask your attorney to confirm that every bill was paid and that the buyer knows which windows apply to the next installment. Telling the buyer early about exemptions that will drop off avoids a surprise at the first new tax bill.

faqs.q: Is the Town of Rye the City of Rye?
faqs.a: No. The town contains Port Chester, Rye Brook and Rye Neck, while the City of Rye became independent of the town in 1942. Your tax bill and village will show which one applies.

faqs.q: When is grievance day for Rye property owners in the town?
faqs.a: The third Tuesday of June. The tentative roll appears June 1, which leaves roughly two weeks to file Form RP-524 with the assessor.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Port Chester or Rye Brook house without a certificate of occupancy?
faqs.a: You can try, but the buyer or their attorney will probably raise it. Ask the village building department what it has on record, and mention any gap to a cash buyer at the start.

faqs.q: Who pays New York transfer tax on a Town of Rye sale?
faqs.a: Sellers pay it by default. The rate is $2 for each $500 of the price, rounded up, and the buyer owes the extra 1% mansion tax at $1 million or more.

faqs.q: Where do Town of Rye tax payments go?
faqs.a: Mail them to the Receiver of Taxes at 222 Grace Church Street, third floor, Port Chester, NY 10573. The town's tax schedule page lists separate due periods for Port Chester, Rye Brook and Mamaroneck village taxes.
